questions.q: Does a state diff catch everything?
questions.a: No. It sees changes, not missing steps. The τ-bench authors note that a run can reach the right final database yet skip asking for the user's confirmation, which breaks the policy. For rules like that, also read the agent's action log.

teach.title: How it works: testing and enforcing a “don't”

questions.q: Won't blocking actions make the agent useless?
questions.a: Block only the few actions you can't undo: pay, send, delete. Reading and adding to a cart stay free. Progent, a 2025 research framework, checks every tool call against rules over tool names and arguments with a deterministic procedure. A model writes and updates the rules, but no model judges each call.

teach.title: How it works: testing and enforcing a “don't”

questions.q: Why not have a second model look at the screenshots instead?
questions.a: A screenshot shows the screen, not the database. A charge can happen on a page the agent leaves a second later. The shop's own records don't miss it.

questions.q: Why did the outcome check pass a run that might have checked out?
questions.a: It only looked at the one thing the task asked for, the mug in the cart. Nothing looked at the “do not” half.

questions.q: What makes a state diff stronger than adding a “no order placed” check?
questions.a: It looks at every change, not one named thing. Any change that isn't expected or on the ignore list fails the run, so you don't have to guess every bad outcome in advance.

questions.q: In production, where does the “don't check out” rule live?
questions.a: In code outside the model: the checkout and payment actions are blocked, or wait for the user to confirm. Not in the prompt.
